items.definition: The power to decide which topics the public thinks about, exercised through selection and emphasis in coverage.
Influence over how a topic is understood: which frames, words and experts define it.
Influence achieved through attraction and information rather than force or payment.
Withholding one's own views to avoid social, professional or legal consequences.
The tendency of a cohesive group to converge on one view and suppress doubt in order to preserve harmony.
A statement that fixes the exact meaning of a word, so that everybody uses it the same way.
items.example: The definition of a tolerance is written at the top of the drawing, and every measurement follows it.

items.definition: A statement that a system takes as true and never proves for itself.
items.example: The axioms are the starting points of the proof, and everything after them is derived.

items.definition: The step that carries you from what is already accepted to what follows from it.
items.example: By logical deduction, the conclusion follows from the premises, and nothing else is needed.

items.definition: A working idea of how something behaves, kept by the writer and never written as a rule.
items.example: The writer has a model of how a nervous engineer behaves, and every scene is built on it.

items.definition: The written record of a reasoning, in which every line follows from the lines above it.
items.example: The proof is short, and any reader can check it line by line.

items.definition: A statement that an argument starts from and takes as given.
items.example: The premise is wrong, so the conclusion is right only in the proof.

items.definition: The property of a set of axioms that do not contradict one another.
items.example: The two rules cannot both be true, so the set of rules is not consistent.

items.definition: The quality of a situation that could happen, even when it did not.
items.example: The story has plausibility, and the details of the rule are still missing.

items.definition: The point of view a story is told from, which decides what the reader can and cannot see.
items.example: From the perspective of the night engineer, the quiet building is the whole story.

items.definition: A place in a text where two meanings are held at once and the reader must choose one.
items.example: The ambiguity in the last line is deliberate, and the reader has to settle it.

items.definition: The meaning a reader gives a result in their own work once they have understood it.
items.example: The interpretation is the last step: the number is correct, and now it has to mean something on the night shift.

items.definition: The ability to make things happen, whether or not the people affected agree.
items.example: The power to shut the line down was in his hands, and it did not need anybody's permission.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.
items.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.

items.definition: Authority whose basis can be named and questioned, such as checked knowledge, a defined role or a rule that applies to everybody.
items.example: It was legitimate authority: she showed the standard and said who had signed the rule.

items.definition: Power that belongs to an office or an organisation rather than to a person, and passes on with the role.
items.example: Institutional power is why the badge opens the door even though the badge is not the man.

items.definition: The pressure to return a favour that the other side has given you.
items.example: The discount was the favour, and the renewal at the same price was the bill.

items.definition: The habit of giving way to authority without asking for the reason.
items.example: Deference is not weakness, but a room full of deference has nobody left to check anything.

items.definition: Any effect one person has on another, from a request to advice, in either direction.
items.example: Influence is not a privilege: the newest member of the team influences the oldest one as well.

items.definition: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.
items.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.

items.definition: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.
items.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.

items.definition: The arrangement of roles that says who decides and who answers for the decision.
items.example: The hierarchy is clear on paper; the account, the invoice and the parts were not.

items.definition: The formal authority to act, together with the limits that bound it.
items.example: His mandate was to negotiate the price, not to sign the contract.

items.definition: The condition that the reasons for a decision are visible and can be checked by the people affected.
items.example: Transparency was missing: nobody could say which number the decision was based on.

items.definition: The rules a decision must follow: notice, the chance to be heard, a written reason and a way to appeal.
items.example: Without due process the decision was final, and there was nowhere to take it.

items.definition: The answer you owe for an act, to the people affected and to the law.
items.example: The mistake was hers, and the accountability was hers as well.

items.definition: The use of pressure, ambiguity or emotion to move a person into a decision that does not serve them, without giving a real choice.
items.example: It was manipulation: he offered her two options and made the wrong one impossible.

items.definition: An honest attempt to win agreement, in which the other person is free to say no.
items.example: That was persuasion, not pressure: he explained the plan and left the decision to her.

items.definition: A push applied to a decision, usually through time or emotion, that makes the choice harder to refuse.
items.example: The deadline is pressure, but you can still say that you need more time.

items.definition: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of harm.
items.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that presents the decisions of other people as evidence for your own.
items.example: The offer came with social proof: nine out of ten customers chose the larger plan.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that puts the decision in the hands of an expert, real or claimed.
items.example: It used authority: the technician said the part was safe, and showed no manual.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that claims the supply is limited, so that waiting looks like a loss.
items.example: The scarcity was easy to check: the shelf held six, not two.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that shortens the time available for checking and deciding.
items.example: The urgency was built to stop a phone call: sign tonight or the price changes.

items.definition: A pressure tactic that raises the cost of a slow decision, so that speed feels like safety.
items.example: The fear in the message was plain: if you wait, you are the one who pays.

items.definition: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, and which is used as a reason to continue.
items.example: The sunk cost of the training was the argument for staying in the job.
